trend_source: A US creator contrasts a 'house poor' buyer who maxes out their loan approval with someone who buys a duplex and rents out one side (301.7k views, 41.2k likes, 6.3k shares). The lesson about buying what the bank approves versus what you can actually carry travels anywhere.
title: The bank approved it. That doesn't mean you can afford it.
hooks: The bank approving your loan is not the same as you being able to afford the flat.
Here is the number most first-time buyers in Singapore forget to check before they commit.
I have seen people get approved for a home and end up house poor six months later.
talking_points: A bank looks at your income to decide what you can borrow, not your real monthly life: groceries, kids, transport, parents.
A rule of thumb many SG planners use is to keep home loan repayments to a comfortable share of take-home pay, so check your own cashflow, not just the max approval.
Build a buffer for the surprises: a aircon that dies, a leaking ceiling, a job gap, so you don't reach for a credit card.
Factor in your CPF versus cash split and remember renovations and stamp duty are on top of the purchase price.
cta: DM me 'HOME' and I'll send you a simple worksheet to check what you can really afford before you sign.
why_it_works: The original crushed engagement because 'house poor' is a fear everyone recognises, and the honest bridge is simply affordability maths, which is core planning work.
how_to_film: Talk straight to camera, hold up a mock approval letter in the first second. Lead with the hook, then count the hidden costs on your fingers. Keep it brisk, around 35 seconds.

title: Finance for the girls, the Singapore edition
hooks: The number of women who tell me they were never taught money is heartbreaking, so let's fix that.
You don't need to be rich to start, you need to start to get rich.
Nobody taught me money either, so here is the starter stack I wish I had at 22.
talking_points: Start with an emergency fund you can actually reach, parked somewhere separate from your spending account.
Understand your CPF before anything fancy: know what the accounts do and check the official CPF site for the current rates.
Consider SRS if you pay income tax, and read up on it on the official source before committing.
Protect the income before you grow it: a basic health and income plan so one bad year doesn't wipe your progress.
cta: Comment 'GIRLS' and I'll send you a beginner money checklist made for Singapore.
why_it_works: The series proves women engage hugely with approachable, judgement-free money content, and a licensed planner can deliver the local version honestly.

title: Your first 20k changes how you feel, not just what you own
hooks: Your first 20k saved hits different, suddenly a surprise bill doesn't ruin your month.
The richest I ever felt wasn't a big paycheck, it was the first time my buffer hit five figures.
People chase their first million, but your first 20k is the one that changes your nervous system.
talking_points: The first real buffer buys you calm: you stop living paycheck to paycheck and start making choices from strength.
Automate it: a fixed transfer on payday into a separate account before you can spend it.
Once the buffer is there, protect it with insurance so an emergency doesn't force you to drain it.
Then let the next dollars work harder through longer-term tools like SRS or investing, within your risk comfort.
cta: What did your first savings milestone feel like? Drop it in the comments.
why_it_works: The clip went off because the feeling is relatable; a planner can validate it and turn the vibe into a concrete savings-and-protect plan.
how_to_film: Energetic, honest, direct to camera. Hit the hook in the first two seconds. Keep the tone celebratory not preachy, around 30 seconds.

trend_source: A finance creator tells the story of Mr Leo buying an 80k parking lot instead of a 320k apartment and clearing stronger cashflow while the land appreciated (62.7k views, 14.2k likes). A story-driven lesson on cashflow versus appreciation.
title: Cashflow or capital growth: the question before you buy any asset
hooks: A man skipped the apartment and bought a car park instead, and the maths is worth hearing.
Before you buy any asset, ask one question: am I buying for cashflow or for growth?
The flashiest asset isn't always the one that pays you best, here's why.
talking_points: Cashflow assets pay you monthly; growth assets rise in value over time, and many good plans mix both.
The headline price is never the real cost: factor in taxes, maintenance and fees that quietly eat your returns.
Costs can change without warning (in the story a tax reassessment hit his profit), so stress-test before you buy.
You don't need property to diversify; think across your CPF, investments and protection as one portfolio.
cta: Save this if you're weighing up an investment, and DM me 'ASSET' to talk through your own mix.
why_it_works: Story-format finance performs, and the honest takeaway (cashflow vs growth, hidden costs) is textbook planning with no product push.
how_to_film: Tell it as a story with a calm narrator voice. Use simple number overlays for each cost. Pause before the twist about the tax reassessment.

trend_source: A US bartender films depositing roughly 8k in cash from six weeks of tips (18.3k views, 1k likes). The ritual of turning irregular cash income into savings is relatable to anyone with variable pay.
title: If your income is irregular, your savings system matters even more
hooks: If you earn in tips, commission or gig work, this savings trick is for you.
Irregular income isn't the problem, having no system for it is.
Depositing a wad of cash feels great, but here's the step most people skip after.
talking_points: With variable income, pay yourself a fixed percentage of every payout instead of a fixed dollar amount.
Split each deposit the moment it lands: buffer first, then needs, then goals.
Build a bigger emergency fund than salaried folks do, because lean months will come.
Set aside for tax and for your own CPF top-ups since no employer is doing it for you.

trend_source: A Singapore creator shares how a supplementary credit card at 18 with no guidance trapped her in a debt cycle until she cut it up (19.6k views, around 7.5x her usual views). A local, honest story about credit card debt.
title: Credit cards are borrowed money, full stop
hooks: At 18 I thought a credit card was free money, and that mindset nearly broke me.
The most expensive lesson most Singaporeans learn is that a credit card is borrowed money.
If you can't pay the full bill, you can't afford what you just bought.
talking_points: The trap is subtle: you empty your account to clear last month's bill, then rack it up again because there's no buffer.
Rolling a balance means paying interest on things you've already used up; check your card's actual rate on your statement.
The fix is a buffer: build a small emergency fund so you never need the card to survive.
Simple rule: if you can't clear the charge in full this month, don't spend it.
cta: Share this with someone who just got their first card.
why_it_works: It's already a Singapore video outperforming its creator's norm, and credit card debt is a near-universal early-adult mistake a planner can address with zero fear-mongering.
how_to_film: Personal and sincere, direct to camera. Open with your own age-18 confession. Slow down on the closing rule so it lands as the takeaway.

trend_source: A US entrepreneur with millions of followers explains why influencers are going back to corporate: their whole income rode on one uncontrollable source (10.4k views, around 5.4x her usual views). A sharp lesson on single points of income failure.
title: One income stream is one bad month from disaster
hooks: Influencers are quietly going back to corporate, and the reason applies to all of us.
If all your money comes from one source you can't control, you're more exposed than you think.
The scariest words in personal finance: my only income is.
talking_points: A single income stream means a layoff, illness or algorithm change can wipe out everything at once.
Protect the income you have first: income protection and critical illness cover keep cash flowing if you can't work.
Build toward a second stream over time, whether that's investments, a side skill or rental.
Treat your money like a business owner would: diversify so no single event ends the story.
cta: DM me 'STREAM' to map out how exposed your household is to one income drying up.
why_it_works: The video reframes a trendy topic (influencers quitting) into income fragility, which is exactly the risk protection planning solves.
how_to_film: Confident, business-tone delivery. Open on the influencer angle to earn the click, then pivot to 'this is all of us' and list the fixes.

title: Delayed isn't denied: the long game of discipline

Delayed isn't denied, sometimes it's just the down payment on a better life.
Missing out at 22 built the discipline that pays me now.

Delayed gratification isn't deprivation, it's choosing your future self over an impulse.
Automate the discipline so it doesn't rely on willpower: pay future-you first every payday.
Use long-horizon tools like CPF and SRS so time does the heavy lifting, and read up on each on the official sites.
